summary: Describes the S/KEY One-Time Password system released by Bellcore. Each login uses a password that works once, so a captured password cannot be reused. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of secret words where each is used just once, so a thief who sees one can't use it again.

questions: how does s/key one-time password work
how does s/key protect against replay attacks
subtitle: Log in with a password that works only once, built from repeated hashing of a secret pass-phrase.

tldr.problem: Eavesdroppers on a network connection can capture a login id and password and replay them later to get into a system.
tldr.mechanism: The client hashes the user's secret pass-phrase plus a server-sent seed many times with a secure hash function, and uses one fewer hash application on each login. The host hashes the received password once and compares it with the previous one.
tldr.outcome: Only a single-use password ever crosses the network, and no secret needs to be stored on the host. It does not protect against active attacks or stop eavesdroppers reading private data.

today: RFC 1760 is an Informational memo describing the Bellcore system as released; the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
Eavesdropping on network connections to capture login ids and passwords, which are used later to get in, is a replay attack. The S/KEY One-Time Password system, released by Bellcore, counters it. Only a single-use password ever crosses the network, and the user's secret pass-phrase never does, even for commands such as passwd or su. No secret information needs to be stored on any system, including the protected host.

The scope is limited. S/KEY protects against external passive attacks on authentication. It does not stop an eavesdropper from reading private information, and it does not protect against inside jobs or active attacks where an intruder can intercept and modify the packet stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Passwords that work only once cannot be reused by a thief who overheard them. They do not hide what you do afterward, though.

sections.title: The Secure Hash Function
sections.content:
A secure hash function is easy to compute forwards and computationally infeasible to invert. S/KEY is based on the MD4 Message Digest algorithm. MD5 was released after S/KEY went into use, but MD4 was kept because of the large number of client programs already distributed. Clients and hosts must use the same hash function to interoperate.

One-time passwords are 64 bits long, which is believed to be long enough to be secure and short enough to enter by hand. MD4 produces a 128-bit output, so the S/KEY hash applies MD4 to a 64-bit input and folds the output with exclusive-or to get 64 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash is like a blender: you can turn fruit into a smoothie, but you cannot turn the smoothie back into the fruit.

sections.title: Generating the Password Sequence
sections.content:
There are three steps: a preparatory step, a generation step, and an output step. The pass-phrase can be any length and should be more than eight characters. It is concatenated with a seed that the server sends in clear text, passed through MD4, and reduced to 64 bits by exclusive-or of the two 8-byte halves. The result is called S. The seed lets one pass-phrase be used on several machines with different seeds, and lets passwords be recycled safely by changing the seed. A seed may not contain blanks and should be strictly alphanumeric.

The first one-time password is S passed through the hash N times, with N chosen by the user. The next is S passed through N-1 times, and so on. An eavesdropper who saw one password cannot produce the following one without inverting the hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with a secret and blend it many times. Each login uses the result from one blend fewer, so the thief who sees today's result cannot work out tomorrow's.

sections.title: Challenge and Six-Word Passwords
sections.content:
Typing 64 bits is error prone, so a one-time password is converted to, and accepted as, a sequence of six short English words of one to four letters. Each is taken from a dictionary of 2048 words, giving 11 bits per word. All hosts and calculators must use the same standard dictionary, which is attached to the RFC.

The host issues a challenge in a standard format that automated clients can recognize: s/key sequence_integer seed. The three tokens are separated by single spaces, and the challenge ends with a blank or a newline.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a long number, you say six little words, like a short silly sentence that is easy to type.

sections.title: Verification and Reinitializing
sections.content:
The host keeps, for each user, the one-time password from the last successful login, or the first password of the sequence set up with the keyinit command. To verify a login it hashes the received password once. If the result matches the stored password, authentication succeeds and the new password is stored.

Because the client's hash count drops by one each time, the user must eventually reinitialize or be unable to log in. With keyinit the pass-phrase, iteration count and seed can be changed. A frequent technique is to increment a trailing digit of the seed and reset the iteration count to a value in the range 500-1000.

The reference implementation includes calculators such as the key command, which can print several passwords at once with -n count to make a paper list, and the termkey TSR program for PCs that finds the S/KEY parameters on screen and types the password into the keyboard buffer.
sections.plainLanguage: The host just checks that the new word, run through the blender once, gives the last word it remembers. When you run out, you pick a new secret and start over.
